    <document rank="0" url="https://medlineplus.gov/braintumors.html">
      <content name="title">Brain Tumors</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Brain Cancer</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Glioma</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Meningioma</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A brain tumor is a growth of abnormal cells in the tissues of the brain. Brain tumors can be benign, with no cancer cells, or malignant, with cancer cells that grow quickly.  Some are primary brain tumors, which start in the brain. Others are metastatic, and they start somewhere else in the body and move to the brain.</p><p>Brain tumors can cause many symptoms. Some of the most common are:</p><ul><li>Headaches, often in the morning </li><li>Nausea and vomiting</li><li>Changes in your ability to talk, hear, or see</li><li>Problems with balance or walking</li><li>Problems with thinking or memory </li><li>Feeling weak or sleepy</li><li>Changes in your mood or behavior</li><li>Seizures</li></ul><p>Doctors diagnose brain tumors by doing a neurologic exam and tests including an MRI, CT scan, and biopsy. Treatment options include watchful waiting, surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack cancer cells with less harm to normal cells. Many people get a combination of treatments.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/childhoodbraintumors.html">
      <content name="title">Childhood Brain Tumors</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Brain tumors are abnormal growths inside the skull. They are among the most common types of childhood cancers. Some are benign tumors, which aren't cancer. They can still be serious. Malignant tumors are cancerous.</p><p>Childhood brain and spinal cord tumors can cause headaches and other symptoms. However, other conditions can also cause the same symptoms. Check with a doctor if your child has any of the following problems:</p><ul><li>Morning headache or headache that goes away after vomiting</li><li>Frequent nausea and vomiting</li><li>Vision, hearing, and speech problems</li><li>Loss of balance or trouble walking</li><li>Unusual sleepiness</li><li>Personality changes</li><li>Seizures</li><li>Increased head size in infants</li></ul><p>The symptoms are not the same in every child.</p><p>Doctors use physical and neurological exams, lab tests, and imaging to diagnose brain tumors. Most childhood brain tumors are diagnosed and removed in surgery.</p><p>Treatment for children is sometimes different than for an adult. Long-term side effects are an important issue. The options also depend on the type of tumor and where it is. Removal of the tumor is often possible. If not, radiation, chemotherapy, or both may be used.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/neurofibromatosis.html">
      <content name="title">Neurofibromatosis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">von Recklinghausen's Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Recklinghausen's disease</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Neurofibromatosis is a genetic disorder of the nervous system. It mainly affects how nerve cells form and grow. It causes tumors to grow on nerves.  You can get neurofibromatosis from your parents, or it can happen because of a mutation (change) in your genes.  Once you have it, you can pass it along to your children. Usually the tumors are benign, but sometimes they can become cancerous.</p><p>There are three types of neurofibromatosis:</p><ul><li>Type 1 (NF1) causes skin changes and deformed bones. It usually starts in childhood.  Sometimes the symptoms are present at birth.</li><li>Type 2 (NF2) causes hearing loss, ringing in the ears, and poor balance. Symptoms often start in the teen years.</li><li>Schwannomatosis causes intense pain. It is the rarest type.</li></ul><p>Doctors diagnose the different types based on the symptoms. Genetic testing is also used to diagnose NF1 and NF2. There is no cure. Treatment can help control symptoms. Depending on the type of disease and how serious it is, treatment may include surgery to remove tumors, radiation therapy, and medicines.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/opticnervedisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Optic Nerve Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The optic nerve is a bundle of more than 1 million nerve fibers that carry visual messages. You have one connecting the back of each eye (your retina) to your brain. Damage to an optic nerve can cause vision loss. The type of vision loss and how severe it is depends on where the damage occurs. It may affect one or both eyes.</p><p>There are many different types of optic nerve disorders, including:</p><ul><li>Glaucoma is a group of diseases that are the leading cause of blindness in the United States. Glaucoma usually happens when the fluid pressure inside the eyes slowly rises and damages the optic nerve.</li><li>Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve. Causes include infections and immune-related illnesses such as multiple sclerosis. Sometimes the cause is unknown.</li><li>Optic nerve atrophy is damage to the optic nerve. Causes include poor blood flow to the eye, disease, trauma, or exposure to toxic substances.</li><li>Optic nerve head drusen are pockets of protein and calcium salts that build up in the optic nerve over time</li></ul><p>Contact your health care provider if you are having vision problems. Tests for optic nerve disorders may include eye exams, ophthalmoscopy (an examination of the back of your eye), and imaging tests. Treatment depends on which disorder that you have. With some optic nerve disorders, you may get your vision back. With others, there is no treatment, or treatment may only prevent further vision loss.</p></content>
